description: Opioid Use Disorder / MAT population — three mutually exclusive treatment pathways. Buprenorphine/naloxone (45% of patients): monthly outpatient MAT visits, F11.20 as outpatient primary. Methadone (30%): daily observed dosing clinic, F11.20 as outpatient primary. Extended-release naltrexone (25%): monthly IM injection, F11.21 (in sustained remission) as outpatient primary. F32.9 (major depressive disorder) is the principal diagnosis for all ED and inpatient encounters — psychiatric crisis is the leading acute presentation in OUD. SSTI/abscess, overdose, and withdrawal are the expected inpatient scenarios. No patient should receive more than one MAT agent concurrently — naltrexone requires opioid-free washout and cannot be co-administered with buprenorphine or methadone.
do_not_flag: No patient receiving both buprenorphine AND methadone — these are mutually exclusive treatment pathways; concurrent use is a critical prescribing error that should NEVER occur
No patient receiving buprenorphine AND naltrexone — naltrexone precipitates withdrawal in buprenorphine patients; concurrent use is clinically contraindicated
No patient receiving methadone AND naltrexone — same contraindication; opioid-free washout is required before naltrexone initiation
Different patients receiving different MAT agents (buprenorphine vs. methadone vs. naltrexone) — this is correct; each patient is on exactly one treatment pathway

F32.9 Major depressive disorder as primary diagnosis for all ED and inpatient encounters — psychiatric crisis (suicidal ideation, acute depression) is the leading acute presentation for OUD patients; F11.20/F11.21 appears as secondary on these encounters
F11.20 or F11.21 as primary diagnosis for outpatient encounters only — this is the intended design; MAT clinic visits are the routine outpatient reason for visit
F11.21 (in remission) as primary for naltrexone cohort outpatient encounters — naltrexone requires opioid-free status; F11.21 correctly represents sustained remission maintained by naltrexone
Multiple F11.x codes coexisting in a patient record — F11.20 and F11.21 may appear together to represent evolving treatment status or different encounter contexts
Opiates screen result as Positive or Negative (qualitative) — UDS in MAT programs is reported qualitatively (above/below cutoff), not as a numeric concentration
Positive opiate screen in buprenorphine or methadone patients — buprenorphine and methadone are opioids that trigger positive opiate screens; this is expected and not a sign of illicit use

SSTI (L02.91 abscess/cellulitis), overdose (F11.120), and withdrawal (F11.23) as inpatient secondary diagnoses — these are the three canonical OUD inpatient scenarios replacing unrealistic TB admissions
High frequency of outpatient visits (monthly) — MAT regulations require monthly visits minimum; buprenorphine/methadone patients have 12-13 visits/year
Naltrexone patients having fewer annual visits (6-7) — monthly injection schedule generates fewer visits than daily buprenorphine or methadone dispensing
Elevated liver enzymes (ALT/AST 57-300 U/L) in patients with HCV — chronic hepatitis C (18% comorbidity prevalence) causes transaminase elevation
Prazosin in patients without hypertension — used off-label for PTSD-related nightmares in this population
Trazodone in patients without major depression — commonly used for insomnia management
Nicotine dependence (F17.x) co-occurring — smoking rates in OUD are 3-5x general population

Rare TB inpatient encounter (A15) in a minority of patients — 18% Hep C comorbidity can trigger the TB/reportable disease inpatient scenario; 3-5 TB admissions in 200 OUD patients is clinically plausible in high-incidence regions

required_drug_classes.rationale: This is a MAT cohort — the defining feature is medication-assisted treatment for OUD. At least 65% of patients should have a MAT medication documented (some patients may have no recorded medication encounter in a given time window).

required_checks: VERIFY MAT exclusivity: NO patient should have buprenorphine AND methadone, buprenorphine AND naltrexone, OR methadone AND naltrexone concurrently. Flag CRITICAL if any patient has more than one MAT agent simultaneously — this is a patient safety concern.
VERIFY that at least one MAT medication (buprenorphine, naltrexone, or methadone) appears in the medication analysis. If none present, flag CRITICAL.
VERIFY that hepatic function labs (ALT, AST) appear in the population given 18% HCV comorbidity prevalence. If no liver function labs at all, flag MEDIUM.
VERIFY that urine drug screen results appear as qualitative (Positive/Negative), not as numeric concentrations. If UDS results are numeric (e.g. 0.9, 1998), flag HIGH.
CHECK that outpatient encounters represent approximately 85-90% of all encounters — this is a MAT population with predominantly outpatient clinic visits.

VERIFY that no patient receives naloxone (rescue) as their only opioid-related medication without a MAT agent also being documented — naloxone-only with no MAT suggests incomplete medication capture rather than a treatment pathway.
